newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Japan sends strong signals to China for improved ties.
newsitem.headline: Japan sends strong signals to China for improved ties.

text.p: Japan sent strong signals to China on Saturday that it wanted to mend frayed ties but stopped short of lifting a sanction it slapped on China after Beijing conducted nuclear tests this year.

Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen in Manila that Japan would send a mission to China this month to approve projects for yen loans worth 580 billion yen ($5.3 billion) until 1999, a senior Japanese Foreign Ministry official said.

No missions to approve projects for the yen loan package, for three years between April 1996 and March 1999, have been sent since China conducted a nuclear test in May, although Japan did not directly describe the lack of such a trip as part of its sanction against China for the explosions.
However, Japan did say that it froze grant-in-aid for 1996- 1997 for China as a sanction over the nuclear tests, the first time Tokyo used aid as a political weapon against Beijing.
After conducting one more test in July, China signed a comprehensive nuclear test-ban treaty.
The two ministers did not discuss the freeze over the grnnt- in-aid, worth some seven billion yen ($63 million) said the Japanese official, who took part in the talks.
The two ministers attended the two-day ministerial meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, which ended on Saturday.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was to meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Sunday ahead of the fourth annual APEC summit at Subic Bay on Monday.
Sino-Japanese ties plummeted this year over a thorny islands dispute and Hashimoto's controversial visit to a Tokyo war shrine in July.
Chinese verbal attacks on Japan became so vexed after July that Japanese Foreign Ministry officials described ties as the worst since relations were normalised in 1972.

Qian told Ikeda that the two countries must continue dialogue on what the Japanese call the Senkaku Islands and called Diaoyus in Chinese. The islands in the East Chnna Sea are also claimed by Taiwan.
"This problem has spilled over our boundaries and also affected the people in Taiwan and Hong Kong," the Japanese official quoted Qian as saying.
The dispute flared up after a Japanese ultra-nationalist group erected a make-shift lighthouse on one of the islands.
Ikeda promised he would make efforts so that this kind of activity will not be repeated, but he did not elaborate, the Japanese official said.
The two ministers agreed that the issue should be resolved through dialogue and that both sides should keep their tempers, the official said.
Ikeda gave assurances that the present Japanese government had inherited the spirit of former Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama's war apology in August 1995 on the 50th anniversary of World War Two.

China was incensed at Hashimoto's visit because no Japanese prime minister had paid homage to the Yasukuni Shrine since 1985. Yasukuni is dedicated to Japan's 2.6 million war dead since the 19th century, including Class-A war criminals like wartime leader General Hideki Tojo.

Despite the quarrels over the islands and the shrine visit, the ministers agreed to open two new negotiations. One will be on fisheries and ocean zoning under the U.N. Law of the Sea convention. The other will be about Japanese chemical artillery shells and bombs left over in China from World War Two, the official said. Both series of talks will take place in December.
